# Watertight bulkheads (`watertight_bulkheads`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by ship_design_caravel_carrack, steamship_screw_propeller
- Core idea: Divide the hull with strong transverse walls into separate compartments, caulked tight, so local damage can be confined and enough buoyancy retained to stay afloat; the walls also stiffen the hull. They must reach high enough above the waterline that water cannot spill over from one compartment to the next when the ship trims down by the head.
- Pitfalls:
  - Bulkheads that stop short of the upper deck (Titanic 1912): water spills over and floods them one by one
  - Cutting doors through them for convenience and leaving them open
  - Ignoring the cost of subdivision in an open cargo hold; walls and openings affect how cargo can be loaded
- History: china: Tang (618–907) – boat from Rugao with nine compartments; standard in Song and Ming junks; europe: 1785 – Benjamin Franklin recommends the Chinese practice; 1790s Samuel Bentham; 1843 Brunel's SS Great Britain; general in iron ships from the mid-19th c.
- Read:
  - Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 part 3: Civil Engineering and Nautics (1971)
  - Benjamin Franklin, A Letter from Dr. Benjamin Franklin, to Mr. Alphonsus Le Roy ... Containing Sundry Maritime Observations, Transactions of the American Philosophical Society 2 (1786), 294–329
